doc.title: Sherrie Maricle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: IAJE's mission and audiences wanting 'Take the A Train'
summary: She says IAJE should help build audiences, and that graduates find audiences want standards, not their out music.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: What’s the IAJE — do they have a mission to increase the audience for jazz as well as the players?

They do have a mission statement but I don’t have it memorized, I don’t know what it is. But I would think that that would be a really important aspect of education. Actually now that you’re mentioning I find it kind of missing from what they’re doing and I think that would be a really important thing for them to take on. And a lot of that comes from the © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

artists too. And this is the other funny part that makes me laugh. You get out of school, you have all these chops and you’re a great player, and then like I said, you go to the audience and the audience wants to hear “Take the A Train” again for the twenty millionth time in their life. They don’t want to hear your new song that’s the coolest harmony in the world. They want to hear “Take the A Train” and they want to hear it straight ahead and so that’s always finding the balance like to keep the audiences interested. And that’s something — I mean when I was in school I wrote the outest music, I made all these recordings with my friends and we thought that oh this is so hip, this is great, we’re going to be it. “Could you play ‘Take the A Train’ please?”
